mainTopic: Stories about whether a wife is forbidden to her husband because of suspicion of another man, and the end of מסכת נדרים (נדרים צא:)
overview: This amud is a run of short real-life cases about whether a wife becomes forbidden to her husband. In the first two, a wife hints that some visiting merchant was with her. רב נחמן rules she is not believed, because she may have 'set her eyes on another man' and wants out of the marriage. In the third, a man secluded with a married woman bursts through a wall and runs off when the owner walks in. רבא rules she stays permitted, because a man who had really sinned would have hidden. In the last case, an adulterer hiding behind a door warns the husband not to eat cress a snake had tasted. רבא rules the wife is permitted, because a man who had sinned would have been glad to see the husband die. The גמרא asks why this is needed, and explains that we might have thought he saved the husband only to keep a forbidden affair sweet. The amud ends with the הדרן closing פרק ואלו נדרים and all of מסכת נדרים.

steps.title: The wife blames the aloe merchants
steps.stepSummary: This finishes a wife's claim from the previous story. She says that if her husband was not the one, then maybe one of the aloe merchants who were just here was.
steps.simpleTranslation: The aloe merchants who were here just now: if it wasn't you, maybe it was one of them.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining a story already in progress. A wife is hinting that some other man, one of the visiting merchants, was with her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If her words were believed, she would be saying she was with another man. That would make her forbidden to her husband. So the question is whether we trust a claim like this.

keyTerms.meaning: Aloe merchants, traders who sell aloe

phrases.english: The aloe merchants who were here just now,
phrases.notes: She is pointing to visiting traders, hinting that one of them was with her.

phrases.english: if it wasn't you, perhaps it was one of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the wife's claim from the story that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wife hints that one of the merchants was with her.

steps.title: רב נחמן: her words have no weight
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that she may have set her eyes on another man, so her claim has no substance.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: She has set her eyes on another man, and there is no substance to her words.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן decides the first case. He rules that we do not believe her, so she stays permitted to her husband.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wife who wants to leave her marriage could invent a claim like this to get free. Because she has a motive, her words cannot forbid her to her husband.

keyTerms.meaning: She has set her eyes on another man (she wants someone else)
Substance, something solid you can hold onto

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the central idea of these stories. A wife's claim that would forbid her to her husband is suspect when she may have a motive to leave him.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said:
She has cast her eyes upon another man,
and there is no substance to her words.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: עֵינֶיהָ נָתְנָה בְּאַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling on the wife's claim.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: She is not believed, because she may want another man. She remains permitted to her husband.

steps.title: A second unhappy wife complains
steps.stepSummary: A wife is upset with her husband. She says he hurt her during relations just now as never before. He answers that nothing happened between them just now.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a woman who was unhappy with her husband. He asked her: What's different now? She said: You never hurt me in relations the way you did just now. He said: That didn't happen just now.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new, similar story and sets up the wife's claim. The husband's denial prepares her next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband says he was not with her just now. That opens the door for her to suggest that someone else was.

keyTerms.meaning: Her mind was at ease (she was content)
Here, a polite way of saying marital relations

phrases.english: There was a certain woman

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא הֲוָה בְּדִיחָא דַּעְתַּהּ בַּהֲדֵי גַּבְרָא.
phrases.english: who was displeased with her husband.
He said to her: What is different now?
She said to him: You never hurt me
in marital relations the way you did just now.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לַהּ: לָא הֲוָה הָדָא מִילְּתָא הָאִידָּנָא.
phrases.english: He said to her: This did not happen just now.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהִיא אִיתְּתָא דְּלָא הֲוָה בְּדִיחָא דַּעְתַּהּ בַּהֲדֵי גַּבְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story that closely parallels the first one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The setup of the second case: she complains and he denies.

steps.title: She blames the oil merchants
steps.stepSummary: She replies that if it was not him, maybe it was one of the non-Jewish oil merchants who were just there.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said: If so, those non-Jewish oil merchants who were here just now, if it wasn't you, maybe it was one of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The wife makes her claim that another man may have been with her. This sets up רב נחמן's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her claim has the same shape as in the first story. If it were believed, it would forbid her to her husband.

phrases.english: She said to him: If so,

phrases.aramaic: הָלֵין נׇכְרִים נַפְטוֹיֵי דַּהֲווֹ הָכָא הָאִידָּנָא,
phrases.english: those non-Jewish oil merchants who were here just now,

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַנְתְּ לָא — דִּלְמָא חַד מִנְּהוֹן.
phrases.english: if it wasn't you, perhaps it was one of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ: אִם כֵּן הָלֵין נׇכְרִים נַפְטוֹיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: She answers his denial by suggesting another man.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wife hints that one of the merchants was with her.

steps.title: רב נחמן: ignore her
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן tells them to pay no attention to her, because she has set her eyes on another man.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to them: Don't pay attention to her. She is one who has set her eyes on another man.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן rules on the second case just as he did on the first. She is not believed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same reasoning applies again. She has a motive to leave her husband, so her claim does not forbid her to him.
steps.whatToRemember: In both stories רב נחמן rules the same way. A wife who hints she was with another man is not believed, because she may want to leave her husband for someone else.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said to them:
Take no notice of her,
she is one who has cast her eyes upon another man.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב נַחְמָן: לָא תַּשְׁגִּיחוּן בַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling on the second story, matching the first.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Her claim is ignored, and she remains permitted to her husband.

steps.title: A man secluded with a married woman flees
steps.stepSummary: A man was secluded in a house with a married woman. When the owner came in, the man burst through the wall of palm branches and ran away.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man was secluded in a house with a woman. The owner of the house came in, and the man burst through the palm-branch wall and fled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new kind of story. This one is about what the man did, not about what the wife claimed. It sets up רבא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being alone together raises suspicion that they sinned. The detail to notice is that he ran out in the open instead of hiding.

keyTerms.meaning: A wall or fence made of palm branches

phrases.english: There was a certain man who was secluded in a house,
he and a married woman.
The owner of the house came in,
the adulterer burst through the palm-branch wall and fled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story about a suspicious situation, judged by the man's behavior.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The setup: a man secluded with a married woman runs away openly.

steps.title: רבא: she stays permitted
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules the woman is permitted to her husband. If the man had really sinned, he would have hidden himself instead of running out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The woman is permitted. If he had done something forbidden, he would have hidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his ruling and his reason. Running away openly shows the man was not guilty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who has actually sinned is afraid of being found and tries to hide. A man who exposes himself by fleeing in the open shows he had nothing to cover up, so we assume nothing forbidden happened.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read the fleeing as a sign of guilt. רבא reads it the other way: a guilty man would have hidden, so running away openly points to innocence.

phrases.english: Rava said: The woman is permitted.
If it were so that he had committed a transgression,
he would have hidden himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules on the story of the fleeing man.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The woman remains permitted, because a man who had sinned would have hidden rather than fled openly.

steps.title: An adulterer hides behind the door
steps.stepSummary: An adulterer came to a married woman. When the husband arrived, he hid behind the door. There was cress lying there, and a snake tasted it.
steps.simpleTranslation: An adulterer came to a woman. The husband came, so the adulterer went and sat behind the door. Cress was lying there, and a snake tasted it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a final story and sets the scene. This detail about the snake prepares the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the hidden man saw the snake taste the cress. A snake can leave venom in food, so the cress is now dangerous to eat.

keyTerms.meaning: Cress (a leafy plant that was eaten)

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא נוֹאֵף דְּעָל לְגַבֵּי דְּהָהִיא אִנְתְּתָא,
phrases.english: A certain adulterer entered to be with a certain married woman,
the husband came,
the adulterer went up and sat behind the door.
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is the corrected wording, meaning 'behind.'

phrases.english: There was cress lying there
and a snake tasted it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא נוֹאֵף דְּעָל לְגַבֵּי דְּהָהִיא אִנְתְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story, again judged by the man's behavior.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The setup: a hidden adulterer sees a snake taste the food.

steps.title: The hidden man warns the husband
steps.stepSummary: The husband wants to eat the cress without his wife knowing. The hidden adulterer calls out and warns him not to eat it, because a snake tasted it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The husband wanted to eat that cress without his wife knowing. The adulterer said to him: Don't eat it, a snake tasted it.
steps.whatsHappening: The story reaches its key moment: the hidden man gives himself away to save the husband. The ruling on this case comes next, so this step sets it up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By speaking up, the man reveals that he was hiding in the house. This is like the previous case: his behavior will be used to judge whether a sin really happened.

keyTerms.meaning: The master of the house (the husband)

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מָרֵי דְבֵיתָא לְמֵיכַל מִן הָנְהוּ תַּחְלֵי
phrases.english: The master of the house wanted to eat from that cress
without the woman's knowledge,
that adulterer said to him:
Do not eat from it, because a snake has tasted it.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מָרֵי דְבֵיתָא לְמֵיכַל מִן הָנְהוּ תַּחְלֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story. The hidden man reveals himself by warning the husband.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The adulterer exposes himself to warn the husband. The ruling on the case follows next.

steps.title: רבא rules the wife is permitted because the man saved the husband
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules the woman is permitted to her husband. If the hidden man had sinned with her, he would have wanted the husband to eat the poisoned cress and die.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: His wife is permitted. If the man had really done the sin, he would have been glad for the husband to eat and die, as the פסוק says: 'For they have committed adultery, and blood is on their hands.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the ruling on the cress story from the previous steps: the wife stays permitted to her husband.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא reads the warning as evidence of innocence. A man who already sinned with a woman is the kind of person who would be happy to see her husband die, as the פסוק links adultery with bloodshed. Since this man saved the husband, we assume he had not yet sinned.

keyTerms.meaning: He would be pleased, it would suit him
As it is written (introduces a פסוק)

steps.whyThisMatters: This uses the same kind of reasoning as רבא's ruling in step 7: how the man behaved tells us whether a sin really happened.

phrases.english: Rava said: His wife is permitted,
for if it were so that he had committed a transgression,
phrases.notes: "He" here is the hidden man, not the husband.

phrases.english: it would be preferable to him that the husband eat and die,
as it is written: “For they have committed adultery and blood is on their hands.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the halachic ruling on the cress story told in steps 8 and 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wife is permitted to her husband, because the man's warning shows he had not sinned.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A man who saves the husband's life is assumed not to have sinned with the wife.

steps.title: The גמרא asks why this ruling is needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says רבא's ruling seems obvious, so why did he need to say it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבא needed to say something that seems obvious. It is setting up the next step, which explains what we might have thought otherwise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saving someone's life looks like plainly good behavior, so the ruling seems to teach nothing new. The question is not attacking רבא. It asks what mistake his ruling protects us from.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious; why say it?

phrases.english: It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether רבא's ruling in step 10 adds anything new.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the חידוש of רבא's ruling, if it seems obvious?

steps.title: We might have thought he warned the husband only to keep the affair going
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that without רבא we might have said the man did sin and saved the husband only so he could keep enjoying the secret affair. רבא teaches that this is not a concern.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: he did sin, and he warned the husband because he wanted the husband to stay alive, so the wife would stay with him as a secret, forbidden thrill, as in 'Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant.' So רבא teaches us that this is not so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by showing the opposite way we could have read the man's warning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There was a real reason to suspect him: if the husband died, the woman would no longer be forbidden, and the 'stolen' pleasure would be gone. The פסוק in משלי says secret, forbidden things feel sweeter. רבא's ruling teaches that we do not read the warning this way. We assume he had not sinned.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces the mistaken assumption)
He teaches us (that this is not so)

steps.whatToRemember: The warning could be read two ways: as saving a life, or as protecting a forbidden thrill. רבא rules we read it in the innocent way, and the wife is permitted.

phrases.english: Lest you say: he did commit a transgression,
and the fact that he spoke to him and warned him
is because he prefers that the husband not die,
so that the husband's wife would be to him
“Stolen waters are sweet,
and bread eaten in secret is pleasant,”
so he teaches us that this is not so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא question in step 11 by showing the opposite reasoning that רבא rules out.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: We might have thought he saved the husband so the affair would stay forbidden and secret, and so more pleasurable. רבא teaches that we do not assume this.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: We do not assume the warning was a selfish move to keep a forbidden affair going. The wife is permitted.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the chapter and the tractate
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula for the פרק ואלו נדרים and for all of מסכת נדרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, פרק ואלו נדרים, and מסכת נדרים is complete.
steps.whatsHappening: This is not part of the discussion. It is the traditional line that closes the chapter and finishes the whole מסכת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הדרן names the last פרק, ואלו נדרים, and announces that מסכת נדרים is finished. It shows our hope to come back and learn it again.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you (closing a פרק)

phrases.english: We will return to you, perek “And These Vows”
and Tractate Nedarim is completed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Formally closes the פרק and the מסכת after the final סוגיא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The end of פרק ואלו נדרים and of מסכת נדרים.
